en: Preface to the Re-engraved Corrected Edition of *The Record Beyond the Kalpa* (Jie wai lu).

I humbly submit that the *Record Beyond the Kalpa* of the Patriarch Zhenxie was once disseminated in China. At that time, there was Chan Master Tongxuan Jing who composed a critical commentary on this record;
the details are recorded in the *Konggu ji*. Furthermore, he collected the "Hot Iron Ball" (re tie wan) dialogue and included it therein.

Regarding the *Fǎbǎdàmínglù* (Great Record of the Brilliant Dharma) and secular works such as the *Yùnsuì* (Rhymes and Auspiciousness), they are referred to as the *Jièwài Lù* (Record Beyond the Kalpa) by Master Chēngliǎo;

thus, one may say they are flourishing. However, the edition published in Japan during the Kōei era contains more than dozens of scribal errors in its characters, and even the preface to the stele inscription at the end has been omitted.
I have long been troubled by this, until this autumn, when through a karmic connection, I was able to obtain it from Huì.
At the Ingaku-in (Mountaineer’s Peak Cloister) of Nittō-ji, I happened upon an ancient manuscript among a pile of moth-eaten volumes. Upon reading it, I found it to be most comprehensive.
Therefore, I have reprinted it for circulation. Examining the preface to the *Taimyō* (Stūpa Inscription), it states that two collections of recorded sayings (*goroku*) are currently in circulation.
It must be that a *Kōroku* (Extensive Record) also exists; if it does, it may well vie with the *Kōchi Kōroku* (Extensive Record of Hongzhi) in its excellence.
Alas! That it was not transmitted to Japan is a regret for my distant descendants.
Now, having gathered these scattered fragments to append them here, I am like one who cannot bear to discard even a single piece of jade from Mount Kunlun.

Furthermore, as when I previously compiled this *Jiewai lu* (Record of Beyond the Kalpa), it was already a mere fraction of what is above; yet even that was but one-eleventh of the thousand or ten-thousand parts. Nevertheless, compared to [the entirety],...
His hundred volumes and thousand sets are no different from a solitary moon amidst the multitude of stars; its radiance shines everywhere—how could it have any limit?

I humbly hope that those rare talents among the distant descendants, like the unicorn’s horn or the phoenix’s down, will uphold and promote this legacy, fanning the ancestral wind so as not to fail the kindness of the ancestors.
May it be as lofty and vast as Mount Sumeru, and may its lingering shade extend over the Sāgara Ocean.
"Profound and vast! Thus it is said.

On the fifth day of the first month of the spring in the *dinghai* year of the Minghe era, the eighty-five-year-old descendant of the thirty-third generation, A-pian-shan (Aspect Mountain), composed this inscription after washing his hands and bowing at Jinlong Xuan on Rui Longshan in Luodong.
Preface to the Record Beyond Time by Chan Master Liao of Changlu in Zhenzhou:
Chan Master Liao of Changlu was a grandson of Fuyong and a son of Danxia; he received the Dharma atop Bowen Peak.
He attained realization through non-attainment. He preached the Dharma by the side of the River Yiwei; he spoke through non-speaking.
Like clouds drifting and waters stilled, those who followed him to inquire about the Dharma were always seventeen hundred people. They heard through non-hearing. I once visited his chamber;
it was profound and empty, like the wordless silence of Wenbo Xuezi or the state of the Layman Vimalakīrti.

He closed his mouth; I was unable to understand him. Yet, observe how he harbors a fine jade within the empty mountains, blending with the autumn moon reflected in the Milky Way—beholding it, it cannot be seen;
speaking of it, words fail. From time to time, he gazes toward the deep curtains within the hall, pitying the fullness of footprints outside the door.
Thereupon, the priceless panacea cleanses his entrails and transforms his bones; in a mere moment, the sick man rises.
It passes away. Every person attains a lightness and ease such that they have never known illness. It is like when thunder and rain break forth and the grasses and trees sprout;
yet in an instant, the sky clears and the rain ceases, leaving no trace at all. The heavens are clear and the objects fresh; the spring rain has served its purpose.

Nevertheless, how could it be merely like this? The wooden cock crows amidst the frost; the stone tiger roars amidst the clouds. Birds sing in the seclusion of the mountains; cicadas chirp in the silence of the forest.
In this world, there are those who can recognize an ox by its horns and a horse by its neighing; such people may perhaps pass through its enclosure.
Written on the first day of the first month in the twenty-eighth year of the Xiangxing era.
Preface by the Layman of Zhongqiao, Wu Min, for the *Record Beyond the Kalpa* of Master Liao of Changlu in Zhenzhou.
Compiled by the attendants Dechu, Gichū, and others.
[Recorded] during the ascent to the hall. A monk asked, "The Buddhas of the three periods turn the Great Dharma Wheel within a mass of flames;
is this truly so? The Master laughed loudly and said, "I, however, have my doubts. The monk asked, "Why do you, Reverend, have doubts?"
[The monk] prostrated. The Master said, "Wildflower fragrance fills the road; the secluded birds know nothing of spring. The monk bowed and said, "Today I have encountered a poisoned hand.
The Master then said, "The eyes of the willows vie for beauty; wind and smoke blend with elegance. Where it has not yet been revealed, the colors of spring shift secretly; there is no sprouting."
At that time, the light of the stream was dyed with darkness; beneath the cold crags, woodcutters sang their songs, and at the wild ferry, fishermen drummed upon their bellies.
Thus it is said: when the Way is correct, the dragon carries a wondrous treasure; when it is biased, the crane roosts in a silver cage.

But tell me, how do you entrust yourself to that which falls neither into bias nor correctness? (After a long silence, he said: "Where all myriad functions cease, a single melody flows without partiality."
Ascending the hall, a monk asked, "As the sutra says, 'In a land infected by poison, not even a single drop of water may touch it. What is the meaning of this?
The Master said, "Only when you have reached the ultimate limit does it permeate your entire being. The monk asked, "Once it has permeated your entire being, what then?
The Master said, "Only then will you know it cannot be shattered."
The Master then said: "Without relying on the tongue to speak, it blazes forth without ceasing. In the profound and secret place, radiance suddenly arises;

when clarity is manifest, all is fused in brilliant purity. If you can cast down your body along with it, following the flow and letting things be as they are, only then will you believe that all manner of calculations are of no avail, and that its functioning is fundamentally without deficiency. Nevertheless, even though it is so, gold dust—"
"Venerable sir! It has fallen into the eyes and become a cataract.
[The Master] ascends the hall. A monk asks, "What is it like when one has brought a lifetime of practice to rest upon the tips of the hundred grasses?

The Master says, "There is no place to hide the body. The monk says, "In that case, the whole world is revealed in its majestic presence. The Master says, "Above all, do not make a face of it. The monk...
The student asked, "If one does not manifest a face or countenance, how is it? The Master said, "The clay ox butts through the clouds atop the ridge. The Master then said:
"There is no place to plant a锥 (chui-pin), so where can one find a place to settle? A blink of an eye is obstructed; how can one deliberate upon it?

Therefore, he holds fast the eyes of heaven and earth, continuous and without leaking even a hair's breadth. He harmonizes with the transformations of creation; his realization is precise and further—"
There is no leakage. At this very moment, how do you entrust yourself to the phrase "breaking the painted jar"? (After a long silence, he said:
"The clouds disperse and the waters flow away; the heavens and earth are silent and empty."
Ascending the hall, he said: "Study the secret intent by the side; wondrously realize the profound principle. The phrase lies before the formless chaos—how could it traverse the paths of this age?
The tongueless person speaks; those without emotion all hear. The universal path flows on without distinction of time; the spiritual pulse streams vast and unceasing.
But tell me, how is it for that which is neither borrowed nor lent? (After a long silence, he said: "Massive and whole, its entirety is revealed."
"Simply this has never been hidden. He ascended the hall.
A monk asked, "If one does not reveal one's style, is it permitted to turn back? The Master said, "The path of the stone woman is not shared with effort.
The monk asked, "What of the matter above? The Master said, "The wondrous lies before a single bubble; how could it be contained?"
The thousand sages’ eyes. The assembly prostrated. The Master said, "I only fear it is not so. The Master then said:
"Where wisdom does not reach, to speak of it gives rise to horns; when the mind is not extinguished, to recognize it brings forth reflections.
Having cast off all layers, a hundredfold and a thousandfold, soaring through the present and illuminating the past, there is originally no deficiency. The wooden cock crows."

The dark clouds over the ocean of existence are severed; as the stone tigers roar, the mountain colors open in splendor. Let us set aside for a moment the state where light and object both vanish—what kind of person is it who does not receive the hand?
(After a long silence, he says: The green pines breathe an ancient air; white-haired, one laughs upon the cold crags.

Ascending the hall, he said: "In the secret place where the wheel of the pivot turns, the numinous grass has not yet sprouted. It overflows the eyes yet does not ascend; by raising an eyebrow, one understands of itself.
Sometimes the meaning arrives while the phrase does not: the white clouds conceal the jade phoenix. Sometimes the phrase arrives while the meaning does not:

the autumn dew drips onto the silver river. Sometimes both meaning and phrase arrive together: the wondrous exhaustion does not belong to the present; the empty clarity does not leave the door. And so it is."
"When neither the Way nor its meaning reach the words, how is it? (After a long silence, he said: "Not transmitted through the mouths of a thousand sages;

do not seek it amidst ten thousand maneuvers. He ascended the hall and said: "In the dark, the transverse bone is drawn out; the all-pervading phrase is already manifest. Sitting with the tongue in the light, it encompasses the earth."
Without patterns or colors, the mixture admits no trace; the illumination leaves no mark. The golden sun emerges from the void at midnight;
thick clouds arise at noon upon the faces of the peaks. Tell me, who is it that carries the burden beyond Mount Sumeru? (After a long silence, he said: Do not travel the path of the profound;
when merit is exhausted, one returns to the ordinary.
Ascending the hall, a monk asked, "What is 'learning that does not stop at noon'? The Master said, "The silver wheel shines from the bottom of the sea.
The monk asked, "What is 'the intention that does not establish the mysterious'? The Master said, "Spring on the trunk of a shadowless tree.

The monk said, "If so, then the unrevealed mechanism attains the wondrous at the very moment of confrontation. The Master said, "That too must be turned back. The monk asked, "After it has been turned back, what then?"
The Master said, "This is a function that does not fall into mere blending.

The Master then continued: "To exhaust the subtle is to lose the root; to contemplate the wondrous is to forfeit the source. A single phrase cuts off the current until the very depths of the stream are exhausted.
Therefore, where the golden needle is held in secret, its brilliance is not revealed; when the jade thread passes through, it silently displays extraordinary luster. Nevertheless,"
It is so. These are both explained through mutual interpenetration. But tell me, when skill and clumsiness do not reach it, how can one entrust oneself? (After a long silence, he said:
"Where the cloud-vines are exquisite, the green shade closes together; when the crag-trees are high, the emerald locks are deep."
Ascending the hall, he said: "To shift function and settle in the position is for one who moves forward; 'Jade hidden in the Jingshan mountains' is precious.
To shift the position and return to function is for one who comes back; 'A flake of snow on a red furnace' is spring. When both function and position are shifted, the entire body is unimpeded.
Letting go of the hand, forgetting all reliance—the stone woman ascends the loom at night; the secret chamber has no one to sweep it. At this very moment, there is no breath."

"How shall one entrust oneself to a single phrase? (After a long silence, he said: "Returning to the root, the wind falls the leaves; illuminating all, the moon-lake is empty. Ascending the hall, he said:
"Discerning the subtle within the coarse, one emerges from within the gate; the stone woman is not alone, for the shuttle and loom leak their secret workings.
Discerning the coarse within the subtle, one exits through the body; though the warmth has vanished, the snow and ice remain upon the crags. The jar is not yet broken—before the kalpa."
Spring. The livelihood of the six gates is cold and desolate; ten thousand acres of lapis lazuli pierce the bones with chill.
But tell me, how do you entrust yourself to the single phrase "a drop of water, a drop of frost"? (After a long silence, he said: Go to the hall and ask the Holy Monk.
Ascending the hall, he said: "Dwelling in motion yet ever tranquil; abiding in darkness yet ever more luminous. Not falling into the mechanisms of the two extremes—who dares to strike at the head?
Pressing straight and lifting from the side, there is a basis for it; true compassion and wondrous response are inexhaustible.

Although these words exist before the sprout has even emerged, they nonetheless do not depart from the present moment. But tell me, in the end, how is it? "White clouds cannot be detained; they rely on—"
Emerging from the ancient blue heavens, he ascended the hall.
A monk asked, "The earthen ox constantly moves its feet; why is it that it is not permitted to touch the waves?

The Master said, "Empty space nods its head in the dark. The monk said, "If that is so, then when the child approaches the father, there is still something upon which to rely. The Master said, "Furthermore..."
There was one person who was unwilling to enter. The Master asked, "I wonder who this person is? The teacher replied, "Red and raw all over the body;
look within the fire. The Master then said:
"When the profound mystery is exhausted, the vision becomes biased and withered; when clarity is unmoving, it leaks away amidst conceptualization."

A thousand peaks pour forth emerald hues; ten thousand valleys flow with spring. The numinous sprouts are exquisite, yet their vital energy has not yet emerged; auspicious radiance divides as heaven prepares to dawn.
Light merges with the moon reflected in water; shadows blend with the empty pool. When illumination accords with the forgetting of traces, how can one distinguish differences?
The wooden dragon chants at midnight—its wondrousness lies in what precedes hearing.
Ascending the hall, he said: "Where the body is hidden, there are no traces; when the vast intent is fused, who can discern it? Where there are no traces, do not hide the body;
where one suddenly shifts their step, the wondrous is difficult to find. Within the withered roots and stones, the flowers are bright and elegant;
beyond the kalpas, the majestic light is dense and ever-new. Therefore it is said: 'For thirty years at Yaoshan, I have clarified only this matter. O virtuous ones!"
"What is this matter? (After a long silence, he said: "White-haired, yet his countenance is like jade; spiritually alert, he does not fall into the present. Ascending the hall, he said:
"The wondrous principle of non-action does not involve the profound and subtle. A single thought secretly penetrates, and the entire mechanism operates in secrecy.
It is easy to play the melody of 'High Mountains and Flowing Waters,' but difficult to transmit the night-bright talisman of empty space. Who can know these spiritual phrases in the dark?"
The majestic light beyond transformation must be seen for oneself. Although it is so, if one does not travel the path of the green peaks, how can one reach the root of the white clouds?

He ascended the hall and said: "The wondrous transformation spreads secretly; from nothingness, something suddenly appears. As soon as the ripples of a bubble are conceived, the profound stillness is lost and the truth is deviated from. Nine.
The night sky is pure, vast and boundless; when the four seas are clear, the bottom is revealed.
If you know this message, you will be able to repay the unrequited kindness. If it is not yet so, then heaven and water blend as one color in autumn;
amidst the gathering stars, the Purple Microcosm stands high.

Ascending the hall, he said: "The sounds of the household are distinct and clear, yet the essential point is difficult to penetrate. To succeed is not a matter of effort; forget the burden you carry. Outside the door, clouds follow along the broken path;
within the assembly, there is no illumination superior to the burning lamp. Since you know that your livelihood is already perfected, you should naturally let it sink deep and fade away.
Why, then, do you still have matters on the road? (After a long pause, he said: "When merit is equal, one transcends through kalpas."
The movement of the steps was not according to the Yang [hexagram]. He ascended the hall.
A monk asked, "If the subtle and dense is already manifest, is it still noble and honorable? The Master said, "Its function lies before the myriad activities;
there is no need to present cleverness. The monk said, "In that case, a single phrase is spiritually resonant, and the common path is cut off at its source. The Master—
The Master said, "Which phrase is this 'Anā'? The monk hesitated. The Master said, "Your transgressions fill the heavens.
The Master then continued: "A single sweep across the dust of the lands; great and small, they measure the void. Eons and thoughts are both fused;

the past and future limits are severed. Without leaving this very place, the perfect response is infinite. Abiding securely within this, one acts everywhere without weariness. At such a time as this, the wood..."
A youth knocks at the moon-gate; the six faculties are empty and luminous. The stone sprout secretly extends its branches; its solitary standard is elegant and dense.
Tell me, whose realm is this? (After a long pause, he says: The wind and waves are swift upon the riverbank; the scenery of the reed village is secluded and profound.
Ascending the hall, he said: "Seeing and hearing are not obscured; sound and form are utterly true. Movement and stillness are without deficiency; going and staying are fundamentally wondrous.

If you can fully take this up and accept it, only then will you believe that every dharma is perfectly accomplished. You will then be able to establish the school wherever you are, returning to the ordinary and harmonizing with the Way.
If this is not yet so, the autumn dew wets your breast; the single mirror is cold and without trace."
Ascending the hall, he said: "Before you have ceased, cease; before you have rested, rest. Suddenly, the precious mirror stands upon its pedestal;
boundless pure light fills the doorway. Therefore it is said: 'One phrase should be luminous, not illuminating; one phrase should be illuminating, not luminous.
But if it were both illuminating and luminous, what then? (After a long silence, he said: "Snow upon the tip of a withered branch."
Awaiting the Great Yangchun (the Great Spring).

He ascended the hall and said: "Do not resent Shitou for his loquacity; he immediately spoke of the clarity of the Lingyuan. Its brilliance is pure and bright, its function perfected so that its illumination never falters.
Its emptiness and subtlety are fully luminous without interruption. Now, as it truly is, it is difficult to conceal; it is entirely leaked away by the autumnal light."
To repay the practitioners within the realm, I shall examine the seasonal timing therein.
[The Master] ascends the hall. A monk asks: "When the midday lamp does not serve as an illuminator, and the night torches fill the sky with red light—what then?

The Master says: "You still fall onto the path of the sidelines. The monk asks: "What is the principle that transcends this? The Master says: "When both light and darkness are exhausted, it is all..."

[The student] said, "It does not illuminate. The Master then said: "Wearing fur, you roam amidst the mass of flames; concealing your body within the fire. Wearing horns, you mingle with the dust and mud;

shifting your steps within the light. The numinous pearl is free of spots; Bian’s jade is without flaw. In a single thought, all is vast and harmonious; a thousand mechanisms blossom forth. It being exactly thus—"
At that time, he stepped aside from the path and said, "There is another who can speak of this. (After a long silence, he said: "Clearly transcending the realm of transformation;
throughout vast eons, its essence remains indivisible."
Ascending the hall, he said: "Before the bright curtain has been rolled up, the secret palace radiates light; the wondrous body is subtly manifest, yet the true mechanism remains profound.
It is such that the dragon roars in the blue sea and the phoenix dances in the crimson sky; the great earth spreads auspiciousness and the vast void arrays blessings.

At this very moment, how shall one entrust oneself to the single phrase of 'Birth by Borrowing the Position'? (After a long pause, he said: "The golden seal has not yet been opened, yet the dust-motes of the dharma realms [are already illuminated]."
Silence. At the place where the jade wheel turns, it does not encounter the wind.
Entering the hall, he said: "Within, it is as bright as the sun; there is not the slightest obstruction. This single spirit does not rely on a womb;
of the four elements, which one is the sovereign? Now, with utter thoroughness, it is revealed in its majestic presence; its functioning follows conditions, always free and at ease. Although...
Yet it is thus; this is still merely ordinary conduct. But tell me, how do you entrust one who transcends the school and surpasses the standard?
Space has no face; there is no need for cleverly painted brows.
Ascending the hall, he said: "To discriminate all day long is merely to discriminate one's own mind.
It is laughable that by recollecting the power of Avalokiteśvara, one ultimately remains attached to one's own person. The old monk Huangtou has reason that is difficult to vindicate.
Why is his reason difficult to vindicate? Because the thief is one’s own kinsman."
Ascending the hall, a monk asked, "When the shadow-grass is not deployed and the thousand paths have ceased their praise, what is the matter within?
The Master said, "He does not sit upright upon the dais. The monk said, "In that case, the full function has been turned over.
The Master said, "Turned where to? The monk said, "The moon is bright at the ancient ford; the autumn colors deepen at twilight. The Master said, "One must indeed be such a donkey."
Han: The Master then said: "People are lost on the path to enlightenment; the door hangs amidst withered trees. Appearance and disappearance blend together; the congealed flow is bright and pure.
The wondrous essence is numinous and leaves no trace; when the entire body is exhausted, it does not face the sun. The sound of water and the resonance of pines—a deep mountain stream."
The moonlight and the ripples of the waves—the entire body is wondrous. At such a time, in whose sphere does it fall? (After a long silence, he said:
"The boat is full and empty, yet not night; when one is securely on the hook."
Ascending the hall, he said: "The rain washes the mani-jewel, increasing its brilliant hue; the entire body is not obscured by even a single thread of hair.

The spiritual source pours forth without ceasing, adding to the waters of Mount Chu so that they flow upstream. Therefore it is said: 'True compassion and wondrous response accord with conditions as they arise.
Within the Great Samantabhadra Light, there is fundamentally no appearing or disappearing. Even so, were it not for ascending the highest peak, how could one..."
Seeing white clouds high above, he ascended the hall and said:
"Mirrors reflecting one another, lights entering one another—these are still matters on the periphery of images.

Appearing at every head and manifesting in every object, such a person is called 'one who has accomplished the task. Even if one does not involve oneself with conditions and does not occupy a position, it is entirely..."

The myriad phenomena blend within a single thought, vast and harmonious; yet there still seems to be something remaining. What, then, is this "different species"? (After a long silence, he said: "In every gate there is nothing hidden;
the wondrous lies in the time before division."
Ascending the hall, he said: "Closely and intimately draw near; from time to time honor and revere him. Thus, filial devotion still remains.

It is only when one no longer perceives drawing near, filial devotion, or honoring and revering that one first attains nobility. Nevertheless, though it be so: let the sun and moon alternate their illumination as they will;
beyond the azure sky and outside the clouds, they do not interfere with one another."
Ascending the hall, a monk asked, "When one does not admire the various sages and does not prize one's own spiritual essence, what then?

The Master said, "Wild grass flourishes before the ancient mirror stand. The monk asked, "If one proceeds in this very manner, what then? The Master said, "The golden crow carries a fragment of cloud."
The Master then said: "Following the current has no fixed stopping place; true illumination leaves no trace. Where a thousand peaks are beautiful, the crane finds it hard to perch;

when ten thousand waters are clear, the fish is naturally at ease. Woodsmen cease their appreciation; fishermen lose their way to their nests. Amidst deep clouds at the ancient ferry, we sing together in a peerless melody.
At such a time as this, where is the one who understands? (After a long silence, he said: The Jade Hare is ever present."
The Fifth Day. The white sun does not shift its wheel. He ascended the hall and said:
"The supreme, pure, and wondrous mind pervades the entire dharma-realm. Its essence is refined and true, vast and open, bright and penetrating.

The numinous flowers bloom densely, surpassing those of former springs; their flavor is perfectly integrated into a phrase beyond the mundane. It reaches the point where the cold forest is arrayed with color, and the wild..."
The flowing water carries fragrance; it is silent and does not stagnate. How could their natures be different? When facing the sun, one does not tread the path of the present age.
Having attained the meaning, there is no partiality; the bird-path is profound.
Ascending the hall, he said: "The sun and moon are eternally vital; from antiquity to the present, they never change. How can one be suddenly new? Each must offer three prostrations.
When the ultimate state of non-reliance is exhausted, the body is naturally profound; do not shout for joy over the double six in the dice game.
How do you distinguish between gain and loss? (After a long silence, he said: "Nine out of ten words being right is not as good as a single silence."
Ascending the hall, a monk asked, "What is it like when one encounters no person on the ancient path? The Master said, "We have been traveling together all along.
The monk said, "If that is so, then one’s entire body appears and disappears within the radiance of the myriad phenomena. The Master said, "You are still a traveler coming and going.
The monk asked, "How is it for one who is not a traveler coming and going? The Master said, "The ancient path cannot be found."
The Master then said: "A single ox drinks water, secretly blending with the clouds over the stream; five horses do not neigh, yet their wind-bone is revealed in the dark.
Setting aside for a moment the fact that it does not fall into the trap of clever wit—it is too subtle and pervasive, too spiritually manifest—how do you interweave [the response]?
(After a long silence, he said: An old silkworm-woman weaves; the shuttle clicks clearly through the night."

Ascending the hall, he said: "The pivot turns within the realm of clarity; the wondrous function is fully exhausted in the shift of the body. A single dream of green mountains; a boat full of white moonlight.

At midnight, the clouds withdraw from the azure sky; on the Mid-Autumn night, the dew blends with the Milky Way. Deep within the reeds, we suddenly meet; laughing and chatting over tea, there is nowhere to hide.
At this very moment, you must further know that there is one person who does not join the company."
Ascending the hall, he said: "The profound mechanism of Vulture Peak and the secret intent of Shaolin are sung together by mountains and peaks, high and low;
they are heard naturally by waters and clouds, coming and going. Those who attain them give rise to horns and tusks in vain; those who lose them find their merit and achievement to be in vain.
Thus it is said: 'Do not seek awakening, for there is originally no delusion. When the sun rises in the east, it sets in the west at night. Although it is thus, yet—"
"What does the Way rest upon? (After a long silence, he said: "No need to refine the nine tripods; the hundred flowers flow anew. Entering the hall, he said:

"Transcending mind, intellect, and consciousness; reaching the source and forgetting emotion. This is the crown of all sages. Pushing aside the myriad phenomena, one thoroughly penetrates the root-source.
One should clarify the hidden illumination; entering the gate, one forgets the way back. The rustic elder sings for joy; the stone man claps his hands. This is the state of true [enlightenment].
At such a time, is there anyone who knows where it has fallen? (After a long silence, he said: "The fragrant herbs of the Snowy Mountains flourish, yet the tracks of the white ox are not seen."

Ascending the hall, he said: "At the tip of every one of the ten billion hairs, flowers bloom; they do not offend the spring breeze. Amidst the snow of the three winter months, they vie for fragrance, fully manifesting the vast intent.
Clouds gather at the break of dawn in the valley; as a drop of water freezes into ice, the livelihood is already perfected. By whom can it be enjoyed? (After a long pause, he said:
Three or five pecks of gray ash upon the head—clearly, it does not fall into the trap of the dawn."
Ascending the hall, he said: "Just so! Cease seeking. It is already manifest and majestic; forget gain and loss.
Even if the mind were to penetrate infinite time, throughout kalpas it has never been different from today. (He laughs loudly and says:
Sitting in the Hall of the Holy Monk, standing outside the Diamond Gate, the broad and long tongue illuminates heaven and earth. At midnight, the crow flies, white as black lacquer."
Ascending the hall, a monk asked, "When skin and flesh have fallen away entirely, and there remains only the single reality, what is the matter within it?
The Master said, "The door is closed; the spring breeze does not lodge overnight guests.
The monk said, "If so, then where the green cliffs embrace the clouds, the secluded moss forms a mound of emerald. The Master shouted, "You still find this insufficient!"
The Master then said: "When not a single thought has arisen, ten thousand miles are without a blade of grass. Where the entire body is crimson and raw, the whole world has never been hidden.
The bird-path forgets its support; the traces of clouds are unique. Even to attain such a state is still to investigate the subtle while losing the source.
Therefore it is said: 'Let all the people in the world rejoice as they may; I alone do not consent. Now tell me, what is it based upon?"
"What is it? (After a long silence, he said: "The fish move, and the sand darkly stirs;
yet they never infringe upon the clear waves. He ascended the hall and said: "Silent radiance is majestic and grand; manifest realization is subtle and dense. The thorough path hides the ultimate;

Epitaph for Chan Master Zhongxian Zhenxie Liao.
The Way reaches the Great Sameness; nature is perfected in perfect penetration. Abiding without abiding, empty without being empty.

East and West, across thirty-three transmissions, they silently accord like the joining of tally-sticks; this proves that faith is not private, but public. The Buddha swallows the three periods of time; the sutras shatter atoms.
One gives rise to the radiance of one's own self and attains the functional pivot of the patch-robed monk. Roots and objects emerge in equilibrium. Practice...

He walked in accordance with nature. He was silent as heaven and earth, yet he brought to fruition the transformative radiance of yin and yang. His vital energy matched that of the four seasons, and his compassion was equal toward the myriad species.
He kept the lamp of the ancestral shrine alight and maintained the discipline within the monastic garden.

Grasping the handle of the Dharma and bearing the burden of the Buddha, he exerted his strength to resist demons and heretics, taking personal responsibility for all hardships. Chan Master Wukong was such a man. His name was Qingliao, and his dharma title was Zhenxie.
His secular surname was Yong, and he was a native of Anchang in Left-Mian. As a child, when he was carried into a temple, his brows and eyes moved with joy upon seeing a Buddha statue;

everyone marveled at this. At the age of eleven, he entered the monastic order under Qingjun of Shengguo Temple, where he studied the *Lotus Sūtra*. After seven years, he passed the state examination and received ordination.

Once he had completed his full precepts, he went to Daci Temple in Chengdu to listen to lectures on the *Awakening of Faith*, the *Vajracchedikā-prajñāpāramitā-sūtra*, and the *Mahāyāna-śraddhotpāda-śāstra*.
Having lectured on the *Śraddhā* Sūtra and other treatises and grasped their essential meaning, he ascended Mount Emei to pay homage to the Great Being Samantabhadra.
Traveling east out of Shu, his path led through Lunan Commandery, where he was invited to stay at Jianchongning Temple. The master said, "The timing for a Kunpeng bird—how could it be so hasty?
He descended the Qutang Gorge, bypassed the Yanyu Rocks, emerged from Jingzhou and Chu, traveled through Mian and Han, and arrived at Dengzhou.
This was the seat of Chan Master Chun of Danxia Mountain. One day, while entering the inner quarters for instruction, Danxia asked, "What is the self prior to the void kalpa?

As the Master was about to offer a reply, Danxia gave him a slap. The Master attained sudden enlightenment. The following day, Danxia presented him with subtle and profound questions to test the depth of his realization;
it was like a pearl’s reflection following its form, or a valley’s echo responding to a sound. Thereafter, he traveled north to Mount Wutai.
He paid his respects to the Great Being Mañjuśrī and subsequently arrived at the capital, where he visited and investigated all the renowned seats of Chan and doctrinal study.

Traveling down the Huai and Bian rivers, he reached Yizhen, where at that time Chan Master Zu Zhao resided; the assembly of "elephants and dragons" from Changlu numbered ten thousand, treading upon one another.

The Master threw himself into their midst; those of noble character and talent drew close to him, and in no time, nearly half of them had joined. He invited [the Master] to serve as his attendant, but after more than a year, he dismissed him and treated him with the status of a *zhuanwu* (a monk in charge of the kitchen).

When the Master was subsequently promoted to share the seat and enter the inner chamber (*rushi*), he silently withdrew and departed. Patriarch Zhao summoned him back with a verse, and he returned to hold the whisk (*bifu*).
As the mature elders of the monastic community flocked to his door and bowed in humility before him, he appointed him as the Head Seat (*shouzuo*). This was in the eighth year of the Zhenghe era.
In the year [of the] *zǔzhào* [cycle], Zuozhao retired from the monastery. That night, he dreamed of a person who told him, "A monk from Shu shall succeed you.

Upon waking, he wondered, "Is it Foguo or Fuyan? Not long after, he was invited once more to preside over the community. In the third year of the Xuanhua era, Zuozhao fell ill; the Master was again appointed as the First Seat (*dìyīzuò*).

When his illness became severe, he retired from the monastery. In the seventh month of the autumn of the fourth year, Public Official Chen, the Commissioner for Military Operations (*jīngzhìshǐ*), invited him.

The Master was appointed as the successor. In the fifth year, on the summer solstice, he resided in the Cloud Hall with seventeen hundred monks. In the fifth month, he ascended the hall to receive the Dharma from Master Chun.
In the sixth month, a river wind drove the tide over the fields, so that there was almost no harvest. The Master ascended the hall and addressed the assembly.
"Sit at ease and do not worry. In the eighth month, Zu Zhao passed away. The Master conducted the funeral rites according to the protocol for a teacher.

In the tenth month, he personally went out to beg for alms. In the second month of the sixth year, he announced his return. He beat the drum to distribute what had been obtained, and the provisions required were more than sufficient.

For over seven years, he had guided others to the source and pointed them toward the origin; he had illuminated the obscure and drawn from the deep. In the sixth month of the second year of the Jianyan era, he retired from the monastery. In the eighth month, he ceased accepting money.

At Tangru, like Meiceng in Ming, he paid homage to Avalokiteśvara Bodhisattva. Of the more than seven hundred households on the sea mountains, upon hearing his teaching, they all abandoned their fishing livelihoods;

in a single day, they saved the lives of hundreds of thousands, tens of millions, and billions of beings. In the fourth month, he passed through my location during the retreat period (*kṣetra-bandha*).

In the fifth month, he was thrice invited and thrice declined by Guoqing Temple on Mount Tiantai. In the eighth month, he went on a tour of Mount Yanwang. In the tenth month, he stayed as a guest at Tian...
He was appointed as the abbot of Fosi. At the invitation of Xuefeng of Shoufu Tang, he entered the monastery on the first day of the eleventh month.
The assembly of monks from all quarters again exceeded the numbers previously seen at Changlu. Lay devotees hastened to offer alms, so that the annual expenditures became ample and prosperous.

Among the Buddhist sites in Min, those that have been Zen monasteries since ancient times are situated in deep forests and remote valleys, with their pavilions and halls facing one another; the leaders who preside over them are all eminent elders of the Way from the rivers and lakes. One—

He washed away his old habits. In the fifth year of the Xiangshu era, he retired to the East Hermitage. In the seventh month of the sixth year, the seat at Guangli on Mount Ayuwang in Siming was vacant;
by imperial decree, the Master was invited to assume the position. The temple was dilapidated and in disrepair, difficult to manage:

the morning and evening bells were not struck, the hearth fires were not lit, and the outstanding debts amounted to nearly two million coins. Everyone was filled with anxiety. On the tenth month, the Master entered the temple.
Villages and hamlets, forests and fields, all rejoiced at the news of the Master’s arrival. Distant relatives and neighbors came from afar, supporting the elderly and leading the young;

their shoulders and heels brushed against one another as they crowded together, and their boats followed one after another like linked vessels. By the time the Master had even begun to warm to his seat, eight or nine parts out of ten of the outstanding debts had been repaid.

He remained stationed in Jiankang for seven years, during which time an imperial decree invited him to reside at Mount Jiang. He declined the summons while traveling and citing illness; only upon his seventh petition was he granted permission. In the eighth year, [he went to] Long... at Wenzhou.

The two monasteries of Xiangxing and Qingxing were merged into a single Chan residence, and the Master was summoned by imperial decree to preside over it. In the fourth month, he entered the monastery and ascended the hall for a small discourse (*xiaocan*).
He gathered and settled the incoming assembly. As the rising tides threatened the eastern and western sites, he constructed embankments and ditches for protection.

On the elevated ground to the south and north, he erected the triple gate (*sanmen*) and the Great Hall (*dadian*). The Dharma Hall and the Abbot’s Quarters (*fangzhang*) were flanked by auxiliary buildings, while gold, grain, bamboo, and wood were sought through alms-gathering.

He attained this realization. A pair of pagodas, exquisitely fashioned as if by magic, rose majestically upon the river. He presented a painting of them to the Emperor, who granted him a thousand *mu* of land.

Once his provisions for the Dharma were fully satisfied, he devoted himself exclusively to the duties of the Buddhas and Patriarchs. In the second month of the fifteenth year, he requested leave to retire from his post.
In the fourth month, an imperial edict appointed the Master to reside at Mount Jing in Lin’an. In the fifth month, he entered the monastery;

the number of monks exceeded one thousand, and as the permanent endowment was meager, he relied on begging for alms to support them. In the second month of the twentieth year, he requested to return to Changlu due to illness.

In the twenty-first year, by imperial decree, the Chongxian Xianxiao Chan Monastery was established; upon its completion, the Master was summoned to preside over the abbacy. In the sixth month, he entered the monastery; however, his illness worsened during the journey in the summer heat.

In the ninth month, on the *rénzǐ* day, Empress Dowager Cíníng visited the temple. The Master, despite his illness, presided over the opening of the hall (*kāi táng*). She raised the curtain to listen to the Dharma;
the exchange of questions and answers during this single session was brilliantly illuminating. She bestowed upon him a gold-embroidered *kāṣāya*, silver, silk, and other items.

On the *guīhài* day, his illness did not improve. On the *jiǎzǐ* day, physicians were summoned, and he recovered slightly. The Cíníng Palace granted funds for the construction of a *shuǐlù* (Water and Land) Dharma assembly.

On the first day of the tenth month in the year Dingmao, an imperial messenger came to inquire after him; they parted with ease. A short while later, he called for the head seat and said, "I am now departing.

He closed his eyes, sat in the full lotus posture, and passed away. His remains were kept in the shrine for eight nights. The Cining Palace sent down incense and bestowed ceremonial silks to accompany the funeral offerings.
It was divined that a stupa should be built in the Peach Blossom Grove to the west of the monastery to enshrine his entire body. This was in the year Renwu.

The remains were enshrined in a stupa. Those who escorted the coffin filled the plains and fields; their hearts were pierced with grief and they shed tears, all sighing that the flowers of the patriarchs had withered and the groves of Chan had fallen into cold desolation.
In the eighth month of the twenty-third year, by imperial decree, he was posthumously titled Chan Master Wukong, and his stupa was named Jingzhao.

The Master’s physical appearance was tall and dignified; though initially emaciated, he later became robust. His eyebrows and eyes were sparse yet elegant, and his spirit was serene and profound. He raised—

In movement he surpassed the soaring clouds; in stillness he stood like a crane. His influence was like a reflection or an echo, his reception of stimuli as clear as a mirror and as empty as a valley.
