It shines radiantly, with not even a hair’s breadth of obscurity. This is the state where quiescence is entirely movement. If you now wish to bring this movement to rest:
They simply retreat to a place of stillness, yet they do not realize that stillness itself turns into movement. O Zen practitioners, stillness is movement;
why do you try to stop it? Therefore, the sage keeps his breast empty and hollow, possessing neither consciousness nor cognition.
Though he dwells in the midst of activity and function, he always abides in the realm of non-action. As for the single phrase "not involving stillness or movement," how would you act upon it?
"How would you say it? [The Master] struck the meditation seat and said, "A hundredfold fragments.
[The student] merely lingers on both sides; how could he know that which is of one kind?
The Master struck him, saying, "It is precisely because this bare lump of flesh seeks to resist my staff that it does not recognize pain and dies beneath the blow."

"Merely clinging to movement and stillness, you delude yourself and pursue external objects. You are carried away by the worldly flux of the sense bases and their objects, whether with form or without form.
When will you ever realize that this matter exists? Do you wish to understand? The monk hesitated.
The Master said, "Even if you were to beat a hundred thousand or ten million people, what would it avail?"
"One kind does not penetrate; at both places, effort is lost.

[The Master] picked up the staff and said: "As expected, leaning on a fence and groping for a wall, their feet are busy and their hands are in disarray. Movement is entirely stillness, and stillness is entirely movement. It is one and without duality.
You, dull-witted and ignorant fellow, since you cannot strike through it, you apply effort toward the place of movement; furthermore, you recognize the thief."

As a son, you have been practicing your craft in a quiet place; yet you are like one who cuts off his own head while seeking to stay alive, doing nothing but falling into pits and ditches—neither achieving the first nor succeeding in the second.
Your understanding is biased and stunted, and your mental state is leaking away. Do not say that you have failed in two places; you have simply missed the mark at every turn.
If you penetrate in one place, you will penetrate a thousand and ten thousand places all at once. Now tell me: is this so?
"That one place. After a long silence, he said: "On the road there are flowers as well as wine; a single journey is divided into two.
He dismisses existence and non-existence, turning his back on emptiness from within emptiness itself.
The Master held up his whisk and said: "What means of salvation is there? Let me ask you: what object do you have that you might dispatch?
Try to bring forth even a single thread or hair for me to see. The entire universe and all the great earth are, in their entirety, this very host.
It is simply the matter of a monk’s daily life; it is called wondrous function, it is called wondrous existence. How would you go about dispatching it?"
If you reject the myriad phenomena and cast off the dusty realm by dispelling all existence, you will become deluded regarding wondrous existence and fall into the view of nihilism.
Zen practitioners, simply contemplate this carefully: if you reject the myriad phenomena and cast off the dusty realm, you fall into the void of the kalpa of emptiness;
yet you turn your back on true emptiness, failing to realize that the very phenomena before your bowl are themselves true emptiness. To touch them—*chù*.
All things are originally without marks. To grasp them crosswise or employ them inversely—what prohibition could there be? For the most part, people do not understand the mind-ground.
To dismiss the myriad existents is to be deluded regarding wondrous existence; to follow the emptiness of annihilation is to turn one's back on true emptiness.

Merely ceasing movement is the dismissal of existence; seeking to return to stillness is the following of emptiness. Within this, one speaks of existence and emptiness; previously, one spoke of movement.
To speak of stillness: movement itself is stillness; existence itself is emptiness. The names differ but the substance is the same; there is no other dharma. Now tell me, where does the fault lie?
One gazes greedily at the moon in the sky and loses the pearl in one’s own hand.
Much talk and much deliberation—these turn out to be inconsistent with one another.
[The Master] says: "Now, lower your voice. The moment you open your mouth, there is no longer any connection. You must lift up the iron hammer without holes;
you must cause all people throughout the great earth to lose their bodies and forfeit their lives. If it were not so, you would strike them as if they were mere hemp.
Within the vine-tangle, it is like a lame tortoise or a blind turtle entering an empty valley; when will you ever get out?
Zen practitioners, if this matter were contained within words and phrases, would the entire Great Canon of Teachings not already be there?

Why, then, was the Flower held up and the Smile given to transmit the Treasury of the True Dharma Eye? Do you wish to understand? Close your leather bags and grasp it directly right here and now! Furthermore—
Do not calculate what came before or what lies ahead; as soon as you deliberate or reflect, you have already entered the ghost cave.

Therefore, when emotion arises, wisdom is obstructed; when conceptualization changes, the essence becomes distinct. You must reach the point where the paths of speech are cut off and the movements of the mind are extinguished.
Ultimately, what kind of matter is accomplished? A night of falling flower rain; the entire city is filled with the fragrance of flowing water.
Beyond words and beyond thought, there is nowhere it does not penetrate.
[The Master] picked up the subject and asked: "From where did you receive this news? After a long silence, he said: "It would be better to cut out one's tongue than to violate the national taboo.
He spoke again: "Ten thousand functions are suddenly severed; even the thousand sages cannot carry it. One regards even oneself as an enemy; as for the Buddha..."
The Patriarch then became his disciple. Deshan and Linji had their staffs and shouts; yet when the mouth opens and the eyes stare, at this point they are of no use at all.
Nevertheless, do not merely guard the green grass in a cold rock cave; sit and watch the white clouds—the Dharma is not something inferior.
"Returning to the root, one attains the essential meaning; following after illumination, one loses the source.

[The Master] held up his staff and said: "If you proceed in this manner, it will leave even the mouths of the Buddhas of the three periods, the patriarchs of the six generations, and all the old monks of the world hanging like flat eaves.
This is already falling into the seventh and eighth stages of error; how much more so when one attempts to clarify the fundamental source, distinguish gain from loss, or engage in debate!"

The root teaching speaks of illumination and function. When will you ever find rest? You, son of the Chan school, if you now intend to open your mouth to discuss and understand through words, you fall into the trap of phrases;
thus you investigate the subtle while losing the source, and your capacity becomes obscured from beginning to end.

This is called "leakage of speech" and is called "losing the source by following illumination. It is merely being carried away by the flow of oral sounds, colors, sights, hearing, and intellectual understanding.
As you are about to depart, consider this: when the ancients said, "Leaves fall and return to the root; when coming, there is no mouth," how could one possibly explain it?
Upon the summit of Mount Sumeru stands a rootless tree; untouched by the spring breeze, its flowers bloom of their own accord.
"In a brief moment of returning-reflection, it surpasses the previous emptiness.

[The Master] remarked: "You are trying to turn back the charges, aren't you? Previously, you said that 'discarding existence and non-existence' was following after emptiness and turning one's back on emptiness.
Now you say that 'in a brief moment of returning-reflection, it surpasses the previous emptiness. I thought this fellow had not yet awakened, but here he is again at the front."

Failing to realize that the myriad dharmas are entirely true, one attempts to dispel existence and non-existence. Now, understand that the very substance of all material phenomena (*rūpadharma*) is itself the truth;
there is no longer anything to be dispelled as "existence. Since you have realized that the myriad dharmas are yourself, not a single dharma can be grasped by the emotional mind.
To penetrate through all differences, it is right here and now. In an instant, colors return to the truth; there is no need to depart from them to contemplate emptiness.
It is precisely within this very body that there is no form; it is called "seeing the mind as one sees form. Therefore, it surpasses the previous emptiness.
When you reach this stage of practice, if the pivot is turned once, then throughout your daily life, everything will roll along smoothly, leaving no room for evasion.
Even if you achieve such a state, you have already buried yourself.
The preceding transformations of emptiness all arise from deluded views.

[The Master] remarked: "If you know for yourself, you will immediately attain it. Up until now, you have merely been turning your back on objects to contemplate emptiness, seeking to clarify and still the body and mind by eliminating thoughts of arising and ceasing.
You saw not even a hair’s breadth of this; you perceived only the voidness of the zenith, nadir, and the four cardinal directions, and you took this to be something extraordinary. How mistaken!
You do not realize that this is what appears through the manifestation of your own thoughts. If one is detached from thought and mind, this emptiness will likewise cease.

Thus, although the conscious mind does not cling to existence, it clings to the transformation of emptiness; even the perception of emptiness arising before the mind is a false manifestation. For this reason, you are in a state of wild confusion, denying cause and effect;
abandoning existence to cling to emptiness is like fleeing a drowning only to throw oneself into a fire. Consider this carefully: it is all one and the same.
Having received it, there is no need to seek the Truth; one only needs to still the views.
[The Master] remarked: "This is a case already established. Why do you seek it? Seeing and hearing are true; sounds and forms are also true. Movement..."
Stillness is true; speech and silence are true. Even today, your seeing, hearing, sensing, and knowing are pure and true.
It extends directly through vast eons, filling heaven and earth, filling the ravines and valleys. Amidst a thousand differences and myriad transformations, the entire body is this single truth.

Without moving a single hair’s breadth, it is manifested all at once, lacking nothing whatsoever. Should you have a perception of emptiness, a perception of Buddhas, a perception of Dharma, or a perception of the One—[it is all this very truth].

Completely sweep away all views and understandings until they are pure and clean. Here, in this state of utter nakedness and vivid clarity, one naturally arrives at the ground of stability and intimacy.
Suddenly, Śākyamuni the Old Man said: "When I do not see, why do you not see the place where I do not see?
How would you respond? After a long silence, he said: "What kind of mental activity is this?"
The two views do not abide; be careful not to pursue them. [The Master] comments:
They still linger on the lips. Here, you must completely cast off both the view of existence and the view of emptiness at once, becoming a person of great non-action.
Do not further recollect, do not further seek. The more distant, the more intimate; the more near, the more...

Far away! As one repeatedly abandons, one repeatedly follows after. Only when one reaches the state where the head is covered in ash and the face is smeared with dust, and in a single thought departs into the profound mystery, will one no longer receive food;
thus, one has already attained the state of the Honored and Noble. How can one avoid falling into this place of the Honored and Noble?
"A single moon rises over the sea; how many families ascend the tower?"
As soon as there is right and wrong, one becomes confused and loses the mind of the Teacher.
[The Master] struck him with his staff and said, "Where have you gone? After a long silence, he said:
"Not to be found at the head of the fragrant grass bridge; last night, as usual, he stayed among the reeds."
He addressed the assembly, saying: "Standing atop the highest peak, he pierces horizontally and vertically through the skulls of the monks of the world.
He sits firmly as the master, such that thousands and tens of thousands cannot ensnare him. Now, like an ox at a feeding trough, he grazes upon the grass."
Squeezing a kitten onto a felt mat; if you ride upon the head of a tiger, both become blind men.
Is there anyone who will not accept leftover soup and rancid rice?
Two arise from the existence of one; do not cling even to that one.
The Master held up his whisk and said: "With whom do you speak? Do you understand?

All emptiness and existence, all movement and stillness, all gain and loss, all grasping and rejecting, all hatred and love, all right and wrong—all of these are nothing other than the Lord of the House, without duality or distinction.
Out of necessity, the ancients called this the 'Great Matter' and the 'Single Path to Nirvana.'"

The Gate: The Dharma of the Expedient Means of the One Vehicle. A single word exhausts the ten directions; a single phrase transcends the myriad phenomena. A thousand phrases and ten thousand phrases are but a single phrase;
a thousand dharmas and ten thousand dharmas are but a single dharma. Even when you reach this one place, you must turn it back.
If you cling to one [aspect], it is merely a tethering stake for a donkey. Therefore, Master Yunmen said:
"Even if heaven and earth were free of the slightest flaw or affliction, this is still a secondary statement (*zhuǎnjù*). Only when you do not perceive a single form is it half-revealed.
You must further know that there is a time for the full revelation. For Zen practitioners, this is indeed a point of great difficulty. Do you wish to understand?
One must perform a somersault before a precipice ten thousand fathoms high; only when the life-root is severed straight down can one attain a slight degree of resonance.
When the single mind does not arise, the myriad dharmas are without fault.
The Master remained silent for a long while, then said: "Mountains are mountains; waters are waters; heavens are heavens; earths are earths. What fault is there?
Putting on clothes and eating food, sweeping the floor and brewing tea, traveling east and playing west, and attending to the calls of nature—what fault is there?"
It is only the illness that is removed, not the Dharma; it is not the person of former times who is changed, but rather one's former mode of practice.
What is your mode of practice right now? Gathering water, the moon is in your hand; playing with flowers, their fragrance fills your robes.
"No fault, no law; not born, not mind. [The Master] picks it up and says:
"A single string passes through them all. One lift and they are raised up. Eight sides are transparently brilliant and peerless.
It has reached the point where even the Great Master of the Third Patriarch has no place to hide his body. Do you people know where this falls? The very best!"
A single line breaks the color of the green mountains.
When the capacity [to perceive] ceases with the object, the object sinks along with the capacity.
The commentary says: "When both light and the object are forgotten, what is it then? Do you know? That which illuminates is the mind; that which is illuminated is..."

The objective realm arises because of the mind; the mind is born because of the objective realm. When the mind is free of thought, the realm is empty; when the realm is devoid of marks, the mind is tranquil.
Thus, the subject can follow the extinction of the object, and the object sinks along with the subject. Reason and wisdom merge in profound accord; neither person nor ox is seen.
Truly, when the peach blossoms have all fallen away, where can one find Lingyun?
The object arises from the subject; the subject arises from the power of the object.

It is said: By what cause is this brought about? If the mind is entirely the object, then the object arises from the subject-object relationship. If the object is entirely the mind, then the subject arises from the power of the object.

If the subject arises from the power of the object, then the object is stripped away but the person is not. If the object arises from the subject-object relationship, then [the person] is stripped away.
People do not seize the realm; therefore, when one is fully within the realm, the realm is not seized. Mountains are green, waters are azure, heaven is high, and earth is deep.

Moving freely in every direction, undergoing a thousand transformations and ten thousand changes—when the mind is total, the entire universe and the great earth are shattered into a hundred fragments.
"If you wish to know these two segments, they are originally one.
The Master struck him repeatedly, saying, "What do you mean by 'two segments' or 'three segments'? You only want to eat blows.
I wish to meet the Patriarch face-to-face; do not say that both person and environment are snatched away, or that the holy and the ordinary are cut off, or that there is neither person nor Buddha."

The trichiliocosm is but a bubble on the ocean; all sages and worthies are like a flash of lightning. Even if you could speak with tenfold mastery, you would still not escape being struck with a staff.
When emptiness is one, it is the same as two, encompassing all phenomena within it.
The Master picks up the staff and says: "Whether there is profit or loss, one does not depart from the marketplace. Whether it be 'thus' or 'not thus,' all is contained within this.
Without marks yet manifesting as marks; without form yet manifesting as form; without action yet acting; without doing yet doing.

Subject and object are identical; environment and mind are one. Illumination and function proceed together; person and environment are mutually non-appropriating. Even so, the staff swallows [the world]."

The heavens and earth have been overturned. From where do the mountains, rivers, and the great earth come? When the kalpa-fire blazes forth and all things, even down to the finest hair-tip, are consumed, the green mountains remain as before amidst the white clouds.
Not seeing the fine or the coarse, how could there be partiality?
[The Master] picked up the staff and said: "When a person is at peace, they do not speak; when water is level, it does not flow. How is it during ordinary times?

Even if one were to stir together the cream, curd, and clarified butter until they become a single flavor, or melt the jars, platters, hairpins, and bracelets until they become a single piece of gold—where heaven and earth share the same root, and the myriad things...
All things are of one substance; they are without faction or partiality, without the refined and the coarse. This is not yet considered extraordinary.
But tell me, you people, what is the extraordinary matter? Mountain flowers bloom like brocade; mountain stream water is as deep blue as indigo.

He addressed the assembly, saying: "A rushing torrent crossing a razor's edge; the simultaneous pecking and striking. Like sparks from flint or a flash of lightning, mastery over killing and giving life is attained.
It is already the case that the rooster freezes atop the tree and the duck freezes beneath the water—this is already losing one’s body and forfeiting one’s life.
Is there anyone here who disregards birth and death? Come forth and see within the thicket of entanglements!"
The essence of the Great Way is vast; there is neither ease nor difficulty. [The Master] says:
"The land is wide and the people are few; those who meet it are rare. After a long silence, he says: "How exceedingly vast and great!
The empty space of the ten directions is born within it, like a single fragment of cloud appearing in the great blue sky. Do you wish to know the true essence of the Great Way? [Zhi]...
The Master said, "It is not separate from sound, form, speech, and language. Now, each of you is able to speak and understand, see forms and hear sounds.
Where, then, is the true essence of the Great Way? Have you not seen when a monk asked Zhaozhou, 'What is the Way?'"
Zhaozhou said, "The one outside the wall. The monk said, "I am not asking about this Way. Zhaozhou said, "What Way are you asking about? The monk said, "The Great Way.
Zhaozhou said, "The Great Way penetrates Chang'an. The old man Zhaozhou’s words were too direct;
the Third Patriarch Master opened his mouth and showed his very heart; Master Zhigong’s tongue had no bone. As for those who come to speak of right and wrong—[they...]
These are not humans; three grass-robbers have been captured all at once. How will you judge them? Send them to the local garrison.
Little insight leads to doubt; the more urgent one becomes, the slower one goes.
The Master held up [the whisk] and said, "Go out and take it for yourself. He added, "Who told you to be in such a hurry?

I have told you that there is nothing to do directly; yet your belly is full of doubt. You refuse to step back and accept it, but instead merely move forward, exhausting your body and spirit, urgently seeking to achieve something.
Little do you realize that the more urgent you are, the slower you become; the more you apply your mind, the further you drift from the truth. Directly—
Even after undergoing refinement through three countless great kalpas, one achieves only conditioned meritorious practices;
yet one does not realize that a single thought-moment of no-mind allows for immediate transcendence of the provisional teachings of the Three Vehicles. Have you not seen Zhaozhou say:

"I have seen hundreds of thousands of people, all of whom are merely seeking to become Buddhas; among them, a person who has reached the bottomless ground is difficult to find. Zen practitioners, how is it with you?
Having attained this, one departs without doubt. After a long silence, he said: "The heavens share with white clouds at dawn; the waters mingle with the bright moon as they flow.
To grasp it is to lose the proper measure; one will surely enter a deviant path.
[The Master] picked up the whisk and said: "Blind fellow! Put it down! This matter is like a great mass of fire: to even conceive of it is to die. What is there [to grasp]?"
Nests, tracks, dependencies, and inclinations—do you now still have these dependencies, tracks, nests, and inclinations?

Your own views have not yet perished; you remain attached to those matters, contending over self and others and seeking victory or defeat. Your nostrils point toward the heavens, yet you refuse to acknowledge all people under heaven.
These are entirely false views; you have been rendered helpless by a mere fragment of Chan and the Way, which has squeezed and twisted you into shape.
A single mass remains here. How could one fail to enter the right path? Last year’s plum blossoms, this year’s willows—their colors and fragrance remain just as they were before.
"Letting go is natural; its substance has neither going nor staying.

[The Master] held up his staff and said: "What is it that you let go of? You must be a person with clear eyes to achieve this. Here, not a single bit of Zen, the Way, Buddha-dharma, or anything extraordinary or mysterious is of any use.
It is simply a matter of sleeping soundly and, as the occasion arises, joining the work party to select vegetables for the meal."
Tea talk. Just let it pass like this. All the old monks of the world who brandish mallets and raise fly-whisks are merely dreaming;
their speaking of Chan and speaking of the Way are all but the ramblings of sleep. Tell me, on what principle do they rely?
What can be made of a principle that exists?
Spontaneity accords with the Way; carefree wandering is free from affliction.
[The Master] remarked: "This realm of great non-action can only be shouldered by one who is a person of great non-action.
The ancients nurtured it and nurtured it until they were pure and simple, like infants who cannot distinguish east from west or north from south. Six.
At the gates of the sense-faculties, rest simultaneously; naturally, there is empty luminosity that illuminates itself.

With clarity, one is free from all discursive thoughts and conceptualizations, allowing the nature to follow conditions as it wills. Thus, the teachings of the Buddha and worldly dharmas do not disturb or confound one another.

The faculties, objects, the four great elements, movement and stillness, speech and silence—all are cast off at once. There is no longer even a hair’s breadth of binding attachment. Day and night, one simply maintains this state of empty leisure.
Furthermore, tell me: what kind of matter has been accomplished? After a long silence, he said: "In the end, the frosty night moon falls naturally into the stream before one.
To fix the mind [on an object] is to deviate from the truth; drowsiness is not good.
The Master held up his whisk and said: "Blind sleeper! Now, within your skull and inside your skin-bag, you are in a state of profound darkness.
From moment to moment there is a continuous flow; from moment to moment it manifests before you. How can you avoid violating the Way of Original Truth?

You call this drinking the wine of ignorance, being intoxicated within the den of sensory objects and afflictions. In a state of deep stupor, you lie upon the Great Dharma-body amidst birth and death."
"A long night. To what time will you reach awakening? Even until the year of the donkey, you have not yet seen it in a dream. It is no good to weary the spirit.
What use is there for distinguishing between the distant and the intimate?
[The Master] said: "Why do you mistake your head for its reflection? As soon as you conceive a thought, you err; how much more so when there is distinction between the distant and the intimate?"
Discrimination, inverted views, grasping and rejecting, and intellectual interpretation—what possible connection can these have with the mind’s path of seeking or the mental faculty’s clutching?
This matter requires only the realization of deluded emotion; one must apply silent observation toward that place where the mind finds no foothold.
Why must you exhaust your spirit and weary your mind with bitter deliberation, remaining in a state of dullness all day long?

Even if you were to practice until Maitreya descends to be born, you would merely have cultivated a bellyful of delusive thoughts. Do not take offense at my warning; I fear it may not be so. As the ancients said:
"To attempt to learn the profound mystery with the intentional mind is much like heading west while intending to go east."
If you wish to enter the Single Vehicle (*ekayāna*), do not loathe the six sense-objects (*ṣaḍviṣaya*).
[The Master] remarked: "What is there to loathe? Within the Buddha-lands of the ten directions, there is only the Dharma of the Single Vehicle.
From where could the objects of the six sense-fields possibly come? Try to pick up even a single hair’s breadth for me to see! Internally, the body; externally, the environment; and the great void."
The earth and all things are manifestations within the wondrously luminous true mind. Thus it is with every atom and every thought-moment;
there is not a single dharma that possesses a fixed self-nature. From where could seeing, hearing, sounds, or forms possibly come?

If you can externally cast off the world and internally liberate the body and mind, you will directly perceive the boundless, perfect interfusion of reality and naturally attain great liberation. All...
"Do people wish to see the Patriarch? The mountain is empty, the wind drops stones; the tower is still, the moon invades the gate.
He addressed the assembly, saying: "The Way has no fixed disorder; the Dharma is free from seeing and knowing. Words and phrases may coincide, yet they possess no substantial form."
The minds of the sages of antiquity were like the bright moon, yet their speech was like that of a drunkard. With flavorless talk, they blocked the mouths of others;

grasping the Vajra sword, they cut through the tangled vines. Every word addressed the immediate capacity of the listener, requiring one to grasp it face-to-face. Is there anyone who can truly believe this?
"The six sense objects are not evil; they are identical to perfect enlightenment.
[Zhaozhou] added, "A single word exhausts the path, tearing asunder past and present. Outwardly, mountains, rivers, and the great earth are not seen;
inwardly, the four elements and five aggregates are not seen. Form is not form; sound is not sound. Hearing is not hearing; seeing is not seeing."
He held up his whisk and said, "Do you see this? Xuedou said, "The staff is dust; what fault is there in that?

Since there is no fault, one ought to discern the host. Therefore, setting aside the sixteen-foot golden body at the heap of refuse, he points directly to the thousand-fathom cliff standing erect upon the bare flesh-ball.
Even if one were to face the four quarters and eight directions from every side—
This is exactly the occasion for a physical confrontation. He then threw down his whisk and said: "I cannot simply impose blind shackles or strike with a blind staff either.
The wise act without contrivance; the foolish bind themselves."

The Master held up the whisk and said, "One indictment covers it all. He added, "Nor should one be careless. Beyond form, sound, smell, taste, and touch—the six external sense objects—there is originally no self-substance;
they are entirely the places where a patch-robed monk turns his body, the places of realization, and the places of attaining the Way.

A man of clear eyes uses them with constant intimacy throughout the day. Being without outflows and unconditioned, what fault could there be? It is only those who do not yet know this that harbor doubt in their hearts."

Regarding external phenomena: when you are bound at once by all the myriad objects before your eyes—sights and sounds that you perceive—you do not realize that the myriad dharmas are fundamentally non-existent and that it is only you yourself who is creating a commotion.
Zen practitioners, whenever you see the ordinary, see the holy, see women, or see men, [recognize this as your own delusion].

All of this is merely delusion and perversion within a defiled mind. To speak according to reality, there is not even a single thread of calculation regarding what constitutes an object or a condition.
It is simply you who create trouble where there is none, seeing ghosts before your own skull and drawing forth all these complications—like a silkworm spinning its cocoon to entangle and bind itself.
Have you not seen how the Fourth Patriarch questioned the Third Patriarch for the sake of liberation?
This is a Dharma gate. The Patriarch said, "Who has bound you? Zen practitioners, how do you understand his saying, "Who has bound you? After a long silence, he said:
"Receive the meaning at the tip of the hook; do not fixate on the zero point of the scale."
In the Dharma there is no separate dharma; yet you delusively love and cling to it.
[The Master] comments: How can you blame others? From birth until death, you are simply this very thing.
A thousand dharmas and ten thousand dharmas are but a single dharma. What difference could there possibly be? You do nothing but cherish this and loathe that.
This one. To cling to this and reject that—since there is already attachment, you are merely grasping at one side and needlessly increasing the realm of dreams.
By using self-nature to wash self-nature, you deviate from the true source. It is all nothing but your own false and inverted delusions. Zen practitioners, how do you understand it?
"The Dharma has no different dharmas. After a long silence, he said: "A single word encompasses the ten directions; not even a hair's breadth is left out."
To raise it up:
To use the mind by means of the mind—is this not a great error?
[The Master] picks it up and says: "How can you blame others? Can your four elements hear the Dharma? Since it is but a lump of bare flesh..."

"You do not understand how to listen to the Dharma. What, moreover, is this 'listening to the Dharma'? At present, you are using the Dharma to listen to the Dharma, seeking mind with mind, and seeking Chan with Chan.
You carry a whole load of Buddha-Dharma and yet come here to seek someone to explain the Buddha-Dharma for you—is this not a great error?
I fear that you will fail to grasp it; do you still have any sense of shame? You have already mounted a cow, yet you come back to ask about it."
"Where are the man and the ox? Do not fail the man.
Delusion gives rise to stillness and chaos; awakening is without good or evil.
[The Master] remarked: "What end is there to speaking of delusion and speaking of awakening? This very thing is present within the possession of every person."
This essence of emptiness and stillness is luminously clear from top to bottom; it is free from fixed disorder and detached from seeing and knowing.

It transcends the ordinary and the holy, and surpasses the realm of emotional and intellectual measures. If one moment of deluded emotion suddenly turns its back on this essence of emptiness and stillness, one is immediately obstructed by scattered thoughts and cannot manifest it before oneself.
If even for a single thought-moment no [delusion] arises, [it remains present] before and after.
The boundaries are severed. To awaken to this essence of empty stillness is called the "ground of ultimate reality," where not even a single speck of dust can remain.
What further good or evil could there be? Yet, how is it when one does not involve oneself in delusion or awakening? One constantly recalls:
"In the third month of Jiangnan, where the partridges cry, a hundred flowers are fragrant."
Regarding all dualistic extremes, he arbitrarily deliberated and remarked:
"Who taught you to wander aimlessly? Now you speak of sagehood and ordinariness, delusion and enlightenment;
you speak of good and evil, existence and non-existence; you speak of stillness and chaos, mind and environment; you speak of gain and loss, and you speak of 'is' and 'is not'."

No. All methods of relative opposition are dualistic extremes. If you use these two extremes to engage in speculative conjecture or arbitrary deliberation, it is nothing but a chaotic display of frivolous distraction.
If you attempt to conceive of it with the mind, you have already missed the connection; how much more so when you resort to opening your mouth?
As long as there are words and phrases, they all lack true meaning. Do you understand? The giant turtle does not dwell within the rivers or lakes.
How laughable are the people of this age who clutch their fishing rods!
Dream-like illusions and empty flowers—what need is there to grasp or seize them?
He says: "Let it go! There is not a single thread of a thing. Why do you generate so many calculations and schemes? One.
All myriad objects are dreams; all myriad phenomena are illusions; all myriad dharmas are flowers in the sky.

Not even a hair’s breadth can be grasped. It is only because your karmic consciousness is vast and murky that you falsely cling to this stinking mass of bone and skull—the fleshly lump of the four elements—as your own self.
This leads to much turmoil, as you spend your days chasing after the myriad objects before your eyes.
One simply continues to wander through the cycle of dreams. How can a seeker of Chan awaken? After a long silence, he said:
"Under the clear blue sky and bright sun, let gain and loss, right and wrong—all at once be cast aside."

The Master held up his whisk and said: "Where would you put it? If there were even a single thing, I would tell you to let it go. But since it is like a dream, an illusion, or a flower in the sky, how can you do so?
Monks, if I now require you to let go of gain and loss, right and wrong, it will truly be a laborious task.
You must have an awakening; once you have awakened, there is no need for you to let anything go. You will naturally know that this is all but a dream."
An illusion. Generally speaking, if the mind is free from affairs, the myriad dharmas are all of one suchness.
If your heart is restless and itchy, with right and wrong, gain and loss, and attainment and failure before your eyes, how will you understand his principle of "letting go of everything at once"?
After a long silence, he said: "If only the snow could melt away, spring would naturally arrive."

He addressed the assembly, saying: "The eye that secures heaven and earth is continuous and does not leak even a hair’s breadth; it is free from the arising of views and emotions, pure and without a single speck of stain.
To deliberate is to err; to open one's mouth is to fall. A blink of an eye or a raising of an eyebrow—ten thousand miles of white clouds."
Having arrived here, how will you turn yourself around and breathe out?
"If the eyes do not sleep, all dreams are naturally eliminated.
[The Master] picks up the phrase and says: "Why this talk in one's sleep? The Buddhas of the three periods of time speak of dreams; the Patriarchs of the six generations speak of dreams. Heaven..."
The Junior Elder says that even speaking of dreams is a dream. Raising an eyebrow, blinking an eye, striking the mallet, or holding up the whisk—all these are merely speaking of dreams.

But tell me, by what cause is this brought about? It is simply because all sentient beings, since beginningless kalpas, have lain their Great Dharma-body within the long night of birth and death, dreaming of undergoing the cycle of birth and death through the six realms. It is like a person in the world who is overcome by deep sleep. Five...

The five sense-faculties are active, and the sixth consciousness, the deluded mental consciousness, falsely perceives various dream-objects. These objects do not truly exist; they are merely transformations of consciousness.
While one is actually dreaming, it cannot be said that they are non-existent. Yet upon awakening, the mind and its objects vanish, leaving nothing at all.
Thus it is said: "Within the dream, the six realms are vividly present; after waking, the great chiliocosm is empty and void."
"You should know that awakening is itself a dream. If the eyes are open and one is not asleep, there are no dream-objects.
If the mind does not arise, there is no birth-and-death. The saṃsāra of the six destinies is entirely created by the mind.
The Great Master, the Third Patriarch, spoke thus; Jikan spoke thus; all of you listen thus. Now tell me: is this a dream or is it awakening? He gave a shout and said, "Be alert!"
If the mind does not differ, the myriad dharmas are one suchness.

[The Master] held up his whisk and said: "I have finished speaking all at once. Do you understand? It reaches the point where movement and stillness are one suchness, and speech and silence are one suchness."

Seeing and hearing are one as suchness; delusion and awakening are one as suchness; sage and ordinary being are one as suchness. All conditions and myriad objects are the total manifestation of the single True Reality.
There are no phenomena outside the mind, nor is there a mind outside of phenomena. You must understand it in this way before you can finally accord with Suchness.
O people: when the eyes sleep, there are dream-visions; when the mind clings, this is saṃsāra. When the eyes do not sleep, dream-visions vanish of their own accord;
when the mind does not waver, all conditions are empty and still. Since from the beginning there has been not a single thing, let the flowers and willows be as green and red as they may;
the warbling of swallows and the singing of orioles are entirely the livelihood of a man of the Way. Even so, it is much like spring.
The intention lies in the scene. Alas!
"One as such embodies the profound. Utterly forgetting all conditions, he says:
"Close up that leather bag! After a long silence, he says: "It is truly a case of trousers without a crotch and pants without a waistband; there is only green on one's head."
Three or five pecks of ashes—have you even dreamed of such a thing?

Even if you cannot distinguish east from west or north from south, and your eyes are like your eyebrows while your mouth is like your nostrils, and you have nurtured yourself to be as pure and simple as an infant—you have still not dreamed of it.
Do you understand? When the wind has stilled, the flowers still fall; when the birds cry out, the mountains grow even more secluded.
Contemplating all phenomena together, one returns to the natural state.

[The Master] picks up the staff and says: "Clearly seeing that there is not a single thing—Heaven and Earth are but a single finger; the myriad things are but a single horse. One embraces the six directions within..."
Within the breast, the spiritual mirror is more than sufficient. It reflects the myriad phenomena within the space of a single inch, yet its spirit remains eternally empty.

Without moving a single hair’s breadth, all things manifest simultaneously; solitary and luminous, it shines alone, remaining serene through kalpas. Returning to the root and the source, one reverts to the origin and restores the life-force.
Only upon reaching this point does one accord with the Way of natural spontaneity and true suchness. If one can act thus, this is truly transcendence.
The house: that by which it is established is obliterated. It cannot be compared or measured.

[The Master] picks up the phrase and says: "If you open your mouth again, what could you possibly do? Therefore it is said: "When the ten thousand phenomena are obliterated, the whole body is revealed."
Manifest. At this very moment, to describe it as a single thing is not appropriate; to call it a single thing is likewise impossible.

Its categories do not align; it cannot be termed "severed"; it cannot be confused with anything else. It spans all time and eternity. It is like a person drinking water: whether it is cold or warm, they know for themselves.
It cannot be explained or shown to others. Will you people understand? "The egret standing in the snow is not of the same color;
the bright moon among the reeds and flowers is not like it."
When stillness moves, there is no movement; when movement stops, there is no stopping.
[The Master] picks up the staff and says: "This little bit is like a great mass of fire; to even attempt to grasp it is to die. How will you go about conjecturing it?"
Do you understand? Stillness is itself movement; even when still, that which is entirely still is movement. Therefore, movement has no characteristic of movement.
When moving, that which is entirely moving is stillness; therefore, stillness has no characteristic of stillness.
Right now, as you employ your faculties of seeing and hearing, and perform all manner of diverse actions—what is this? If you can perceive it, its very substance is formless.

To have no trace or mark is to be in motion yet without the characteristic of motion. Although it has no shape and leaves no trace, it nevertheless constantly supports heaven and earth within the midst of activity;
this is to be still yet without the characteristic of stillness. If one speaks of its movement, it resembles the mechanism of an iron ox;
if one speaks of its stillness, it manifests form in response to things. It cannot be described through the dual extremes of motion and stillness.
To speculate upon this: for this reason, since ancient times, the Buddhas have closed their chambers and ceased their words, not daring even to breathe.
Were there to be a single breath between them, white clouds would stretch ten thousand miles;
if duality is thus unformed, how could unity possibly exist?
The Master said: "I have already picked it up and finished with it. To say that movement and stillness are two is not the point of contact;
to say that movement and stillness are one is also not the point of contact. Master Xiuzhou said: 'Two, when broken, do not become one; the single Dharma remains forever.

If a person understands this point by the numbers, they will suffer in the depths of samsara for eons. You must know that this matter is beyond conceptual proliferation; there is no place for you to open your mouth. Utterly naked."
Naked and starkly exposed; upon this mass of raw flesh, it stands sheer like a cliff a thousand fathoms high. Do you see it? After a long silence, he said:
"It is right here within these mountains; the clouds are so deep that its location is unknown."
He addressed the assembly, saying: "One whose field of practice is secure and profound is like a langur monkey hanging from a branch—no trace remains.
One who sports with supernormal powers is like flowers blooming on a withered tree, uniquely welcoming the colors of spring.

Suddenly, if one were to spread a net that covers the heavens and employ the mechanism of a pitfall for tigers, you would see it fall apart in every direction. Is there anyone here who can penetrate through the thorns?"
"Linji said: 'To the very bottom, to the ultimate limit—do not maintain any rules or regulations.

[The Master] remarked: "At the top of a hundred-foot pole, how does one advance further? To reach the place of ultimate realization, where words are exhausted and principles are fully realized, the body..."
When the power of effort is exhausted, in the place of profound ultimate depth, there is not a single thread of mystery or subtlety; there is not a single thread of the extraordinary;
there is not a single thread of Buddhist principles or logic. When the Great Function manifests before one, what rules or regulations are there?
Sweeping the floor, brewing tea, threading a needle, mending robes—wearing clothes and eating food according to one's lot is sufficient to repay the unrepayable debt of gratitude. Furthermore...
What Chan is there to investigate? What Way is there to study? Nevertheless, one must truly reach this state before it can be attained.
When the mind accords with equality, all that is done comes to rest.
The Master held up the whisk and said: "When the water rises, the boat floats higher; when the mud is deep, the Buddha is greater. Wherein lies inequality?
If you can penetrate this and see through it thoroughly, you will be able to employ this mind with impartiality. From beginningless kalpas, delusive madness and inversion will naturally cease;
whether speaking or remaining silent, moving or still, there will be a continuous, uninterrupted flow, with every thought-moment dwelling within and remaining ever-present."
All that was done and all that was intended suddenly ceases; the myriad objects and myriad differences are cut off at once.
Each and every thing returns, being entirely the power of one's own effortless, wondrous functioning.
If you can discern this, truly you will not fall short of others. If it is not so, you will expend great effort hereafter.
Doubts are completely purified; right faith is straightened and harmonized. [The Master] says:
"Do you recognize it when it breaks through the gateway of the face? I have told you clearly—why do you not know where it lands?
It is only because there is 'Chan' in your belly that you are not at ease. You must now simply..."

To stuff the wondrous sayings and profound koans of the ancients into your belly, thinking that your lifelong study of the Way is thereby complete—little do you realize that these are nothing but stubborn saliva and snot.
The ancients called this "carrying in dung," which defiles the field of your mind.
To speak with absolute truth, there is not a single drop of ink here; if you harbor even a single character of the original text, you will remain a wild beast for ten thousand kalpas.
A fox-spirit! A clever fellow, upon hearing this, would spit it all out at once, thoroughly washing his natural mouth clean and leaving his mind utterly empty and bare.
Naturally, he would have no doubts; opening his mouth, one would see right into his gallbladder.
You usually say, "I trust him," but you merely maintain this stance without having attained realization; it is not true faith. Do you wish to understand? On the riverbank—
A scene worthy of painting at evening: a fisherman, having donned his single-layered raincoat, returns home.
*All things are left behind; there is nothing to be remembered.* [The Master] picks up the phrase and says:
"Even if mountains were piled high and peaks heaped up, how could they not be left behind? Do you know where it lands? You must simply be empty."
With the depths of one's chest hollowed out, being without consciousness or cognition, one is like a person who has died the great death—like a wall, a tile, or a pebble.
One is consistently devoid of thought and devoid of recollection, without even a trace of breath. The life-root is severed right here and now;

thus, although one is throughout the day amidst movement and activity, one naturally and constantly dwells in the realm of non-action (*wuwei*). After a long silence, he said: "It is not appropriate to speak in such a manner."
"Empty clarity illuminates itself; there is no need to exert mental or physical effort. [The Master] adds:
"Withdraw your tongue and present something else for us to see. After a long silence, he says: "This realm is not something anyone can recognize.
It is not a matter of you temporarily applying some intellectual reasoning and taking that to be the truth. The ancients rested here; they came to rest."
His mouth is like a fan in the month of waxing; his mind is like withered wood and cold ashes. Ten times he speaks, nine times he stops.
Friends, this is not a matter of forced effort; it is simply natural spontaneity. Wherein lies the mystery?
The river moon shines, the pine wind blows; throughout the eternal night and clear sky, what is there to do?
"A realm beyond deliberation; the consciousness and emotions find it difficult to fathom.

"This is not a place for discursive thought. The Gatekeeper said, "The consciousness and emotions find it difficult to fathom. Xuedou said, "This monk did not run when going downhill; Yunmen’s swift opportunity is hard to encounter.

Yet, one has still not seen the Third Patriarch in a dream. But tell me, where does the point of advantage or disadvantage lie? [Shadow] *Note: The term "Ying" (影) at the end likely indicates that this is a fragment or a specific commentary on the "Shadow" section of the text.*
Shaking the thousand-fathom [staff], dragon and snake stir; its sound shakes the heavens, cold as wind and rain.
He addressed the assembly, saying: "The hidden and the manifest are fully encompassed within this ready-made koan; high and low are universally responded to, inexhaustible in daily life."
In vain they boast of the mechanism for subduing currents and sweeping away shadows; in vain they speak of the sharpness of the blade’s edge. Binding grass together fails the will of the Way-man;
carving sand yields no discourse on engraved jade. One must be a person of the "upward direction" to clearly understand matters of the upward direction.
Is there anyone who has penetrated the barrier?
*Tathatā-dharmadhātu*: neither self nor other.
[The Master] picks up the staff and says: "Do not babble! What kind of matter is this? Who taught you to speak like that? Some say: "Non-delusion is called *tathatā* (Suchness);
non-changing is called *tathā* (Thus). The one mind is the *dharma*; its differentiation according to conditions is the *dharmadhātu*. This—
The single essence of True Suchness (tathatā) being unchanging is the Dharma-realm of Principle; its differentiation according to conditions is the Dharma-realm of Phenomena.

The principle being uninterrupted within phenomena is the Dharma-realm of the Non-obstruction of Principle and Phenomena; each and every phenomenon being interpenetrating and inexhaustible is the Dharma-realm of the Non-obstruction of Phenomenon upon Phenomenon.
If you provide such an interpretation, you will not see the Great Master of the Third Patriarch until the year of the donkey.
"I grant you this. An ancient said, "The lush green bamboo is all True Suchness (Tathatā). But how is it so?

Have you not seen how the Abbot of Yanguan asked a Dharma Master, "What sutra are you lecturing on? The Master replied, "The Avataṃsaka Sūtra. The Abbot asked, "How many kinds of dharma-realms (dharmadhātu) are there in the Avataṃsaka?
The Master said, "Briefly explained, there are four; extensively explained, they are infinitely layered and inexhaustible. Thereupon, the Abbot held up his whisk.
The Master said, "This one here—what number is he? The host was at a loss. The Official said, "To know through thinking and to understand through deliberation is like a solitary lamp beneath the sun;
indeed, it fails to illuminate. Do you all understand? Where a single move is missed, the entire board is spent in vain effort.
"Urgent correspondence; it is said that there is only non-duality.
[The Master] picked up the phrase and said: "Even this is still considered insufficient. As soon as it falls from the lips, it becomes a gate of death; there is no path of life.
This very phrase is one that the thousand sages cannot open their mouths to speak. Even with all one’s might, one wishes to say it, yet one cannot say it; one cannot express it."
It is attained. One does not see Mañjuśrī asking Vimalakīrti, "What is the Dharma-gate of non-duality? What did Vimalakīrti say to him?
It was such that his eyes were fixed and his mouth agape, planting his feet squarely on the ground.

The boundless Dharma-gates and boundless wondrous meanings were all realized at once, without missing even a single point. Nevertheless, one must further know that there is a person who laughs "he-he."
A great laugh. If you can recognize this person, you will surely never have to pay for sandals.
"The non-dual is identical; there is nothing it does not encompass.
[The Master] picked up his staff and said: "Swallowed in one gulp, there is no further leakage. Even the wondrous virtues as numerous as the sands of the Ganges are all contained within it."
A hundred thousand rays of light all arise from this. All phenomena are equal; all Buddhas are identical in their Way.

Entering the Dharma-door of non-duality, the holy and the ordinary share the same essence. Encompassing the great void and containing the myriad phenomena, it resides only in the present standing-place of each person.
Without moving a single hair’s breadth, everything is manifested at once. To accept it in such a manner is already to miss the point. It is beyond.
"In what place? Where the power of Yu does not reach, there the sound of the river flows on and on.
All wise ones of the ten directions enter this school.
[The Master] remarked: "Not a single monk in the world can leap out of it. Even the Buddhas of the three periods of time and the six patriarchs enter this school."

The Master entered this school; all the elder monks of the world have entered this school. They manifest great spiritual powers and perform great Buddha-works: sometimes striking with the staff or shouting "Ho!";
sometimes performing dances, rolling balls, raising fly-whisks, or clenching fists; sometimes dragging stones or moving earth.
Every word and phrase, every pivot and every situation, all emerge from this school. Even if one were to respond and adapt through every exit and entry, [it would still be within this school].
It is inexhaustible; this is also what Zhoupo brought to its ultimate conclusion.
The essence of the school is neither contraction nor extension: "In a single thought-moment, ten thousand years. [The Master] picked up the phrase:
"Divine light from ten thousand miles penetrates from top to bottom. If it is contracted, it is but a single thought-moment; if extended, how could it stop at that?
Ten thousand years. Even before the empty kalpa, even further back than that, it does not depart from the daily activities of the present moment.

If one can contemplate that vast antiquity as being just like today, then past and present will be unified, beginning and end will be identical, internal and external sentiments will vanish, and the three periods of time will be utterly purified.
A single length of white silk, a single thought spanning ten thousand years—this is merely a matter of the same hue as an unperforated iron hammer.
You must know that beyond the clouds, atop a thousand peaks, there stands a spiritual pine, cold with dew.
Neither abiding nor non-abiding. [The Master] picks up [a flower] before his eyes in the ten directions and says:
"Spiritual activity, whether still or moving, is all at once enveloped. Even if your mind pervades the ten directions, there is no dharma before your eyes;
it does not abide in any place, yet its intent is right before your eyes. If you can cut it off all at once, there is neither far nor near."
Neither abiding nor non-abiding; whether grasping or releasing, letting go or capturing—it does not depend on another, but is simply one's own inherent supernatural power and transformation.

If one can personally realize, personally employ, personally bear, personally carry, and personally make a livelihood of this, then one cannot be ensnared by nets nor turned back by calls; thus one is able to pass through the net like a golden fish.
"Liǎn has attained great mastery. But what if it is neither a function of the present moment nor a matter of the present moment?
How then? As the assembly hesitated, the Master said, "Quickly, prostrate three times."
He addressed the assembly, saying: "Only by acting among those of different species can one understand the dharma-preaching of the insentient.
When the life-root is severed, one naturally cannot be deceived by others. To open the gate of the empty kalpa, one must pull the boltless lock.
At dawn there is no concealment; at midnight it is perfectly clear. Without cause, the painted cake is shattered, and thus one sees all this mess. Is there anyone [who can do so]?"
"Can it be washed away?
The smallest is the same as the greatest. When the false is severed, there is no objective realm.
[The Master] remarked: "How truly extraordinary! Is the staff small or is it large? When held up, it pervades heaven and covers the earth."
Filling the valleys and filling the ditches—is this not the ultimate identity of the smallest with the greatest?

Upon the tip of a single hair, the void and the great earth appear all at once—is this not the ultimate identity of the smallest with the greatest? Turning the Great Dharma Wheel while seated within a mote of dust;
even the boundless seas of fragrant water and the lands of the Jewel King manifest vividly upon a single hair-tip and a single mote of dust.
Is this not the ultimate small being identical to the great? To casually raise a single finger and fill the void, boundless and shoreless—is this not the ultimate small being identical to the great?
Furthermore, how can one explain the principle of the cessation of delusion from its very sphere of experience?
After a long silence, he said: "Dharma did not understand. Great difficulty, great difficulty!
The immense is identical to the minute; one does not see its boundaries or surface.
He then added: "This great matter—something that the great earth cannot support and empty space cannot contain—is right here."
People say that in the eyes there is "seeing" and in the ears there is "hearing. Is this not a case of the great being identical while the small differs?
The faculty of sight pervades the entire Dharma-realm; the faculty of hearing also pervades the entire Dharma-realm. What boundaries or limits can there be?
To speak according to reality, the entirety of the worlds of the ten directions is nothing but a single brazier, nothing but a single staff—residing right here upon the eyebrows of all people.
Above the eyelashes—is this not a case where the great is extreme and the small is minute? That ancient master said to you:

"The entire earth, gathered together, is as large as a grain of millet. He tossed it before you; yet the lacquer bucket does not understand, and as before, it extends vertically and horizontally throughout all space.
Do you understand? "The village wine is delicious beyond the bridge; the wild flowers' fragrance reaches across the bank."
Existence is precisely non-existence; non-existence is precisely existence.
[The Master] held up his staff and said: "One admission is enough to bring about the consequence; do not further deliberate on what came before or what lies ahead.

In this very same way, one speaks: 'The nature of language is empty; existence and non-existence cannot be apprehended. Furthermore, it is said that existence and non-existence are merely names—they are all conceptual discriminations. My mouth..."
The very place where you raise [this question] is it; how could there be a second? Furthermore, from what place do "existence" and "non-existence" arise?
You merely continue to recognize the sounds and forms of words. If you understand it in this way, you will enter hell like an arrow.
It is just as when a monk asked Zhaozhou, "Does a dog have Buddha-nature? Zhaozhou said, "Yes. The monk said, "If it has it, why..."
"Right then you ran headlong into this skin bag. Zhaozhou said, "Because he knew it and yet committed the offense.
Again, a monk asked, "Does a dog have Buddha-nature or not? Zhaozhou said, "No. The monk asked, "All sentient beings possess Buddha-nature; why does a dog have none?
Zhaozhou said, "Because it still possesses the consciousness of karmic activity (*karma-vijñāna*). Nowadays, my brothers all say that [the answer] lies in the latter part.
This is a concealed expression; the crux lies entirely in the matter of existence and non-existence. Alas! To extinguish the Hu lineage—what relevance does that have?
Do you wish to see the Third Patriarch, Zhaozhou? Gather up your poetry and books and return to your old courtyard: falling flowers and singing birds are one and the same spring.

"If it is not like this, you certainly must not maintain [this view]," he said, adding, "It is still a bit short of the mark; yet I grant you that you possess one eye. He further said, "In such a way, in such a way:
the True Person of No Rank constantly enters and exits through the gate of the face. Without day or night, without movement or stillness, he advances in every thought-moment."

It manifests before you in every thought-moment; it is associated with every thought-moment and guarded in every thought-moment. Whether existence or non-existence, they are naturally strung together as one.
If you are like a mad dog chasing a clod of earth, following words to produce understanding, you are merely pulling down your house and scattering your home, falling into the present moment.
You will be unable to correspond with the master. How can you avoid falling into the present moment? (After a long silence)
It is said: "The moonlight is seen in stillness; the sound of pines is heard in the clear night.
One is all; all is one. [The Master] picks up the verse and says:
"The tongue has no bone; let it pass through every hole. Seize it, and you take the life-force of all people in the great earth!"
It requires nothing more than a single phrase. Some say: "One" is the one mind; "all" is the myriad dharmas. The myriad dharmas are but the one mind; the one mind is entirely the myriad dharmas.
For now, let us rejoice that there is no connection [between these views and reality]. If you lecture in such a manner, you may well serve as a master of treatises;
yet, within the school of the patch-robed monks, even after a hundred thousand million years of further study, you would still not be permitted entry. For now, just stop.
"What is the matter within the gate of the patch-robed monks? Stepping upon the sounding block, it is as hard as iron.
If you can simply act in this way, what need is there to worry about not reaching completion?
[The Master] added: "There is still one more move lacking. As for the ultimate matter, how is it? Many Chan practitioners say that "one" is...
All and all is one. Phenomena (*dharma*) are the mind, and the mind is phenomena.
Simply understand it in this way, and the business of study will be fully accomplished. Do not misunderstand! These patriarchs were people of great non-action;
what use would they have for so much internal entanglement? How do you understand what he said?
"If one can simply act like this, what need is there to worry about anything not being accomplished? After a long silence, he said: "The three men have taken a tortoise and turned it into a turtle.
Regarding "Faith is non-dual" (*xinxin buduì*), the *niàn* (pointer/commentary) says:
"It puts people to shame. He also said: "What do you know of good and evil? You want me to chatter on before your skull!"
What is the Ground? Is it not that faith and mind are one and the same, with nothing further between them?
Do not speak such inverted words. It is thus, it is thus: "Every branch of coral supports the moon. If you can penetrate this and see through to the bottom, you need only this:
"The mind of faith is non-dual; non-dual is the mind of faith. You will then directly encompass heaven and earth and firmly grasp the world. Although...
It is indeed so. If one cannot find flowing water, one must still pass over other mountains.
The path of language is cut off. [The Master] let out a single sigh and said:
"The Third Patriarch, Great Master, has broken his bow and exhausted his arrows. Although this was his final, total presentation, it was received [by the Fourth Patriarch].
A single defeat at the barrier is no small matter. If you can examine it thoroughly, then even when words are exhausted, the sentiments of mountain clouds and ocean moons will be revealed.

If you cannot examine it, then as before, you will not understand and it will fly away again. Some people then assert that where the path of speech is cut off, there is neither past, future, nor present;
they claim this is "the ultimate Way is not difficult, only it dislikes discrimination. The ultimate Way is not difficult... [only it dislikes discrimination].
